To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the dissonance and the self-perception theories of cognitive change both make predictions that are consistent with the data; (2) the dissonant and self-perceived effects were found to be additive in the case of the attitude-change paradigm; and (3) in the case of attitude-change, dissonance and perceived self-change effects were not found to be additive

(a) there is a significant relationship between the number of times a student has been involved in counterattitudinal behavior and his/her level of self-perception, (b) there is a relationship between the number and type of counterattitudinals and self-perception, but it does not hold for all students, and (c) there is a difference in self-perception between students who have been involved in counter-attitudinal behavior in a classroom and in a non-classroom setting
the disconfirmability of a theory is not a function of the number of operational definitions of the theory, but of the logical structure of the theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the level of disconfirmability of a theory and the ability of a theory to account for a phenomenon.
the relationship between the level of disconfirmability and the degree of acceptance or rejection of a theory.
the relationship between levels of disconfirmability and the development of social psychological theories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dissonance and the self-perception approach are both conceptually disconfirmible.
the dissonance and the selfperception explanations of counterattitudal advocacy are not operationally, but conceptually disconfirmible.
dissonance and the self-perception theories have been shown to be conceptually and operationally disconfirming and that they are, in principle, testable in crucial experiments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dissonance and the self-perception theories are complementary, rather than competitive.

we have demonstrated that the disconfirmation of a theory is not dependent upon the operational definition of the theory, but rather upon the empirical evidence which is used to disconfirm the theory.
the dissonance theory and self-perception theory are not mutually exclusive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the disconfirmability of a theory should not be confused with the disconfirmability level of the operationalizations used to test it.
the level of disconfirmability of a theory is not a good measure of its scientific status.
, although disconfirmability is an important criterion in theory construction, it is not the only criterion.
